Start here

The shortest route from “I recognize it” → “I can predict it.”

Your repeatable reasoning chain

1. Identify the two compartments→ 2. Find ΔP→ 3. Apply Fick variables→ 4. Ask whether equilibrium occurs→ 5. Decide diffusion vs perfusion limitation

One question to keep asking: Does the gas still have a partial-pressure gradient at the end of the capillary?

  • Yes → diffusion-limited: the barrier/diffusing capacity is the bottleneck.
  • No → perfusion-limited: the gas equilibrated; more uptake needs more fresh blood.

Fick explorer

Diffusion rate ∝ (ΔP × Area × Solubility) / (Thickness × √MW)

Mechanism explorer: Why disease can make O₂ diffusion-limited

Step 1: Start with healthy O₂ transfer. Alveolar PO₂ ≈100 and incoming venous PO₂ ≈40 → a strong driving gradient.

Step 2: O₂ crosses the surfactant/fluid layer → type I epithelium → basement membranes/interstitium → capillary endothelium → plasma → RBC.

Step 3: In health, capillary PO₂ reaches alveolar PO₂ at about 1/3 capillary length. The remaining capillary length is a diffusion reserve.

Step 4: Fibrosis increases diffusion distance. Emphysema decreases exchange surface area. Both lower diffusing capacity by different Fick variables.

Step 5: If O₂ no longer equilibrates by the end of the capillary, a ΔP persists → under those conditions O₂ behaves as diffusion-limited.

Step 6: Supplemental O₂ raises alveolar PO₂ → increases ΔP → increases the driving force across the abnormal barrier.

Gas & condition guide

The lecture’s models and what each one teaches you.
O₂ — normal lung

Perfusion-limited

  • Incoming capillary PO₂ ~40
  • PAO₂ ~100
  • Equilibrates by ~1/3 capillary length
  • After equilibrium, more uptake requires new blood
Trap: O₂ can become diffusion-limited in disease even though normal O₂ is perfusion-limited.
CO

Diffusion-limited model

  • Very high Hb affinity
  • Bound CO contributes negligibly to dissolved PCO
  • Capillary PCO stays low
  • ΔP persists along the capillary
Therefore: uptake reflects diffusion capacity, which is why CO is used for DLCO.
N₂O

Perfusion-limited model

  • Does not bind in blood in the lecture model
  • Dissolved PN₂O rises quickly
  • Equilibrates early with alveolar PN₂O
  • More uptake requires more perfusion
Emphysema

Surface-area failure

Alveolar membrane destruction and bullae reduce the total area available for diffusion.

↓ Area → ↓ DL

Pulmonary fibrosis

Distance failure

Scarred/thickened interstitium increases the diffusion path between alveolus and blood.

↑ Thickness → ↓ DL

CO₂

Small gradient, fast diffusion

ΔPCO₂ is only ~5–6 mmHg, but CO₂ is much more soluble and has a diffusion coefficient about 20× that of O₂.

Lecture figures

Interpret first. Source details appear only after reveal.

Figure challenge 1

Question: One panel keeps a driving gradient across the full capillary; the other reaches equilibrium early. Which panel represents diffusion-limited exchange, and what feature of the curve proves it?

Panel A is diffusion-limited: capillary partial pressure never catches alveolar partial pressure, so the shaded ΔP persists. Panel B is perfusion-limited: capillary partial pressure reaches alveolar partial pressure early, eliminating ΔP.
Source after reveal: Respiratory_lecture_3_gas_exchange_POST.pptx, slide 18. The lecture uses CO for A and N₂O for B.

Figure challenge 2

Question: Why does the disease tracing fail to reach alveolar PO₂, and why is the failure worse at high altitude?

Fibrosis increases diffusion distance, flattening the rate at which capillary PO₂ approaches PAO₂. At high altitude, PAO₂ is lower because barometric pressure is lower, leaving less driving pressure; the diseased capillary may finish without equilibrating.
Source after reveal: Respiratory_lecture_3_gas_exchange_POST.pptx, slide 19. This is the lecture’s core demonstration that O₂ is normally perfusion-limited but can become diffusion-limited in disease.

Exam sheet

Compact final pass.

Numbers to know

  • Dry inspired PO₂ ≈ 160
  • Humidified tracheal PO₂ ≈ 150
  • Alveolar: PAO₂ ≈ 100, PACO₂ ≈ 40
  • Incoming mixed venous: PvO₂ ≈ 40, PvCO₂ ≈ 45–46
  • ΔPO₂ ≈ 60; ΔPCO₂ ≈ 5–6
  • DCO₂ ≈ 20× DO₂
  • Normal O₂ equilibrates by about 1/3 capillary length

Core Fick rules

  • ↑ ΔP → ↑ diffusion
  • ↑ area → ↑ diffusion
  • ↑ solubility → ↑ diffusion
  • ↑ thickness → ↓ diffusion
  • ↑ molecular weight → ↓ diffusion tendency

Emphysema: ↓ area → ↓ DL

Fibrosis: ↑ thickness → ↓ DL

Limitation logic

Gradient persists → diffusion-limited.

Equilibrium reached → perfusion-limited.

  • CO = diffusion-limited model
  • N₂O = perfusion-limited model
  • O₂ = normally perfusion-limited; disease can make it diffusion-limited

Exam traps

  • PO₂ reflects dissolved O₂, not Hb-bound O₂.
  • Pulmonary artery blood is anatomically arterial but has venous gas composition.
  • Small CO₂ ΔP ≠ poor diffusion; CO₂ is much more soluble.
  • High altitude lowers barometric pressure, not the ~21% O₂ fraction.
  • Supplemental O₂ helps diffusion limitation by increasing ΔP.
